tasks.title: think up contract for new housemate so they can't stay over the test period
suggestions: Drafted a trial-period housemate agreement below — the key clause for your concern is #4 (no automatic continuation past the test period without both of you confirming in writing). This is a plain mutual-understanding document, not a legal lease, but it is the kind of thing Australian share-house arrangements commonly use to set expectations and it gives you a clean, agreed exit point if it does not work out.

--- DRAFT: Housemate Trial Period Agreement ---

1. Parties & dates: [Your name] and [housemate's name], trial period from [start date] to [end date] (recommend 4-6 weeks — long enough to know if it works, short enough that a bad fit does not drag on).

2. Rent & bond during trial: [amount] per week, due [day]. Bond of [amount] held by [you / a bond authority] — specify whether it is refundable in full if either party ends the trial early through no fault of the other.

3. House rules reference: trial is conditional on following the existing house rules (chores, guests, noise, shared costs) — attach or list them so there is no ambiguity about what "working out" means.

4. End of trial — THE KEY CLAUSE: the trial period ends automatically on [end date]. Continuing to live in the property after that date requires a NEW, separate written agreement signed by both parties. Silence, continued rent payment, or having moved belongings in does not extend the trial or create an ongoing tenancy — this is the line that stops someone just staying on by default.

5. Early exit: either party may end the trial early with [7-14] days written notice (text/email counts), no reason required. Bond handling on early exit specified in clause 2.

6. Not a substitute for a lease: if you decide to continue after the trial, you will both sign a proper share-house agreement or add them to the lease/bond at that point — this document only covers the test period.

One thing worth deciding before you finalize: what specifically counts as bond-forfeiting behaviour vs. a no-fault early exit (e.g. property damage vs. just personalities not clicking) — spelling that out in clause 2 avoids a dispute later if the trial ends badly.

⚠ Not legal advice — for actual bond handling and tenancy-law specifics in your state, a quick check against your state's residential tenancies authority (e.g. Fair Trading / Consumer Affairs) is worth doing before you both sign, especially around bond lodgement rules if any money changes hands formally.

claudeNotes.text: ✓ Actioned 2026-09-23: drafted a full trial-period housemate agreement (dates, rent/bond, house rules reference, early-exit terms, and the key clause that stops the trial silently becoming permanent) — see suggestions. Flagged that it is not legal advice and to sanity-check bond rules against your state's tenancy authority before signing.

tasks.title: look into whether this is this best kit for me to sequence my dna https://get.sequencing.com/kitspecials/

noteItems.text: is this a good option for sequencing? are there better ones

suggestions: Short answer: yes, it's a legitimate, reasonable option — not a scam. It's clinical-grade 30x whole genome sequencing (cheek swab, no blood draw) run at a US-based CLIA-certified/CAP-accredited lab, and delivers standard files (BAM/VCF, FASTQ on some tiers) that any bioinformatics pipeline can read. Independent review score: 83/100 (genomereviews.com) — strong on value (90/100) and reports (92/100), weaker on privacy (70/100, its lowest category).

The kitspecials page bundles: Rare Disease & Carrier Screen ($399, was $539, 7-8wk turnaround), Comprehensive Health Screen ($599, was $859, 4-6wk), Professional Health Screen ($999, was $1,699, 2-3wk + 1-on-1 coaching), or a Build-Your-Own from $399 with 40+ selectable health areas. All include 15,000+ condition analysis, AI health reports, and their 'Privacy Forever' data-ownership pledge.

Where it's weaker: Sequencing.com's real product is more of an app marketplace than a single report — 100+ third-party analysis apps of varying quality with no editorial curation, and privacy risk grows with each app you install from an unvetted developer. Budget for that too: meaningful analysis beyond the base kit usually means $5-99 per paid app, so a realistic first-year total if you run 3-5 apps is more like $450-700, not just the $399-599 sticker price.

Direct alternatives if you want to compare: Dante Labs is cheaper on flash sales (as low as €169, ~$185, vs €399 standard) with the same 30x depth and free FASTQ/BAM/VCF — but it's an Italian lab with an 8-12 week turnaround AND a BBB 'F' rating, which is a real red flag on customer service/fulfillment reliability, so the lower price comes with more risk. Nucleus is positioned as having the cleanest UI of the mainstream options if user experience matters more than price/speed to you (no clear public sequencing price found, would need to check directly). SelfDecode is NOT a sequencing provider — it's an analysis tool you upload existing raw WGS data to (from Sequencing.com, Dante Labs, etc.), with the strongest ACMG-based variant reporting (imputes up to 80M variants at 99.7% accuracy) — worth considering as a second step after sequencing rather than as an alternative to it.

Bottom line: for your first WGS kit, Sequencing.com's discounted bundles (especially the $399 Rare Disease/Carrier Screen or $599 Comprehensive) are a solid, low-risk pick given the US lab accreditation and 90/100 value score — just be deliberate about which third-party apps you install afterward given the privacy score. If raw price is the only thing that matters and you're comfortable with a longer wait and a lab with a poor service rating, Dante Labs' flash-sale price is cheaper for the same 30x depth.

claudeNotes.text: ✓ Actioned 2026-09-24: researched Sequencing.com's kitspecials bundles (legit, 83/100 independent review score, pricing/turnaround per tier) and compared against Dante Labs, Nucleus, and SelfDecode — see suggestions for the recommendation and trade-offs.

tasks.title: Huu long on the 21st of Oct?

noteItems.text:
We will get back to Hanoi probably on the 20th. maybe go for the climbing day on the 21st to Huu long and then either stay one night there or head back for the evening too. 


help me work out what the climbing there might look like. what the best transport there would be and whether we should stay somewhere there for the night (find awesome places for 4-5 people to stay) before heading back to Hanoi on the 22nd.i

suggestions: What the climbing looks like: Huu Lung (Yen Thinh commune, Lang Son province, ~110km/2hrs north of Hanoi) is a limestone sport-climbing area developed by VietClimb since 2012 — 250+ bolted routes across 18 crags within a 5km radius. Wide difficulty spread, e.g. Head Wall alone has 23 routes from 5c to 7a, so it suits a mixed-ability group of 4-5, not just experts.

Best transport: book VietClimb's own shuttle rather than DIY — the drivers don't speak English and meeting points aren't well signposted. Two of their partner homestays run direct shuttles from Hanoi: Mao Homestay's shuttle departs 490 Minh Khai daily at 9am/4pm (~3hrs, ~250,000 VND, confirm via Zalo +84 813071992), Duc Bungalows' shuttle departs Gia Lam bus station at noon (~160,000 VND, drop-off 2.5km from the homestay, confirm via +84 965060090). The 9am Mao shuttle gets you there early afternoon — best fit for a single climbing day on the 21st.

Where to stay for 4-5 people: go through VietClimb directly rather than a generic homestay — climbing is literally their business, so booking gets you accommodation + local route beta + gear rental + the shuttle all in one. Their two partner homestays (Mao and Duc, both above) are built for climber groups. If you want a nicer/more independent option instead, May Retreat (~12km from Yen Thinh, lakeside, sleeps up to 16 with extra fees) or Phong Son Retreat (bungalow-style, ~10min from Yen Thinh) both come up well for groups, but you'd need to sort your own transport to/from the crags from either.

Suggested plan for your dates: back in Hanoi ~20th, VietClimb 9am shuttle on the 21st to Mao or Duc, climb that afternoon, stay the night (worth it over a same-day return — 3hrs each way makes a there-and-back day trip tight for actual climbing time), head back to Hanoi on the 22nd. Book directly via vietclimb.vn or their Facebook page (facebook.com/VietClimb) since availability for a group of 4-5 is worth confirming ahead, not turning up on spec.
Nothing bookable on your behalf here (no payment/booking access), but this is enough detail to message VietClimb directly and lock in the 21st.

tasks.title: buy plug adapter
suggestions: Australia's Type I plug won't fit Vietnamese sockets, so you do need an adapter (voltage isn't an issue — Vietnam runs 220V/50Hz, same as Australia, so no separate voltage converter needed, just a plug shape adapter). In Hanoi/northern Vietnam specifically, outlets are mostly European-style Type C/F (two round pins) rather than the flat-pin Type A more common in the south, so get one that covers C/F, not just A.

Easiest single buy: JB Hi-Fi's "Terminal 2 Outbound Travel Adaptor with 4 USB Ports for Europe, Russia, Vietnam & More" — explicitly lists Vietnam, covers the C/F pin shape, and the 4 USB ports mean everyone in your group of 4-5 can charge phones off one adapter if you're sharing a room, so you likely only need 1-2 of these rather than one each.

Alternative if that's out of stock: JB Hi-Fi also stocks the Jackson-brand outbound/international adapters, or a universal world adapter set on Amazon Australia (search "universal travel adapter Vietnam" — several listings explicitly cover EU/Vietnam/Thailand/Bali in one kit, useful if you're stopping elsewhere too).
Nothing purchasable on your behalf here (no payment access), but grab one from JB Hi-Fi in person or order online before you fly — don't rely on finding one easily in Hanoi itself once you land.

tasks.title: buy pool balls for the small table
suggestions: Check your ball size before ordering — small/mini pool tables commonly use either 38mm or 50-52mm balls, not the standard 57mm size, and a set that doesn't match your pockets/rails won't work. Measure an existing ball or the pocket opening if you're unsure which size your table takes.

AliExpress search pages to browse once you know the size: aliexpress.com/w/wholesale-mini-pool-balls.html (mini/38mm-range sets) and aliexpress.com/w/wholesale-mini-billiard-balls.html. Look for phenolic resin sets (more durable, truer roll than cheap plastic) with 16 balls (15 numbered + cue ball); many listings include a mini rack too.
Nothing purchasable on your behalf here (no payment access) — once you confirm the size, picking a highly-rated seller with resin balls and ordering directly is a 2-minute job.

look up if i should get insurance and if so what ones
suggestions: Short answer: yes, get travel insurance for this trip — you have deep water soloing booked (a separate task on this tracker) plus general climbing/cable car/boat activities in Cat Ba, and standard travel policies typically exclude these unless you add adventure-sports cover specifically.

CORRECTION (2026-09-29): I initially said World Nomads' Epic plan covers deep water soloing — that was wrong, misread their activity list. World Nomads marks deep water soloing with an (X), which in their key means excluded from ALL plans, not just gated behind a higher tier. Regular rock climbing/bouldering IS covered (up to 8,000m on Epic, 6,500m on Explorer), but DWS specifically is not insurable with them at any tier.

Who actually covers DWS: BMC (British Mountaineering Council) travel insurance does cover deep water soloing and is considered the go-to for climbers doing this activity — but it's only sellable to UK/Channel Islands/Isle of Man residents, so not available to you directly.

No confirmed Australian-accessible insurer covering DWS by name was found (checked Allianz AU, Cover-More, Fastcover, World Nomads AU — none list it). Before buying anything, call/chat the insurer directly, say 'deep water soloing' explicitly, and get written confirmation — climbing forums report that cheaper insurers often say yes to 'climbing' generally but then deny DWS specifically when asked.

Practical options: (1) still buy a solid policy (World Nomads Epic or similar) for the rest of the trip — flights, general climbing, cable car, boat travel, theft/illness — and treat DWS as a specific gap to self-insure or accept the risk on; (2) ask Vietnam Expeditions/Cat Ba Pathfinders (the DWS operator from your other task) directly whether their tour price includes any accident cover, some operators do; (3) keep checking — dedicated expedition/climbing insurers (e.g. Campbell Irvine, Snowcard) sometimes cover DWS on request even without being climbing-specific brands, worth a direct enquiry if this matters enough to you.

Coverage levels worth checking regardless of DWS: aim for at least $100,000 emergency medical and $250,000 medical evacuation for Vietnam — evacuation (e.g. to Bangkok/Singapore) is the expensive part if uninsured.

UPDATE (2026-09-29): checked, and Vietnam Expeditions/Cat Ba Pathfinders DOES include travel/accident insurance in their DWS tour price (listed as 'Bảo hiểm du lịch' on their tour page). The specific figure — compensation up to 100,000,000 VND per case (roughly USD $4,000) — is confirmed in writing on the OTHER operator's site, Cat Ba Climbing ('Mr. Zoom'): catbaclimbing.com states "All our tours include travel insurance with coverage of up to 100,000,000 VND per case," referenced on their homepage and their Deep Water Solo tour listing. Vietnam Expeditions/Pathfinders' page confirms insurance is included but doesn't state the exact VND figure on-page — worth asking them directly if you go with them instead. Either way, that's real but modest cover — enough for a serious local injury/treatment, not enough for a major medical evacuation, so it's a supplement to your main travel policy, not a replacement.

Practical conclusion: the DWS gap is smaller than it first looked. Buy a solid main policy (World Nomads Epic or similar) for everything else on the trip; rely on whichever DWS operator's built-in ~$4,000 cover for the DWS session itself; if you want it in writing, ask them directly (Pathfinders WhatsApp +84 388 044 501, or Cat Ba Climbing via catbaclimbing.com) for the actual policy terms/limits before you go, since a website claim isn't the same as reading the certificate yourself.

Sources: worldnomads.com/usa/travel-insurance/activities/rock-climbing, ukclimbing.com/forums (deep water soloing travel insurance thread), thebmc.co.uk/en/rock-up-abroad-with-bmc-travel-insurance, worldnomads.com/au/travel-insurance/activities, catbaclimbing.com (100,000,000 VND/case figure), vietnamexpeditions.com/vne_tour/deep-water-soloing-leo-nui-nhay-bien-2
